newsitem.title: USA: Senate committee to investigate Gulf War logs loss.
newsitem.headline: Senate committee to investigate Gulf War logs loss.

text.p: The Senate Veterans Affairs Committee will investigate a Defense Department disclosure that it has lost most of its logs on war gas attack alerts during the 1991 Gulf War, its staff director said on Friday.

Staff director Charles Battaglia said the loss of the logs would be investigated by a special team the committee is setting up to investigate the government's handling of thousands of Gulf War veterans who became sick.

The committee's chairman, Sen. Arlen Specter, a Pennsylvania Republican, has said the special team will investigate whether the Defense Department tried to cover up information that might explain some of the illnesses, but he said he was not accusing the Pentagon of a coverup.

The Defense Department gave the Senate Armed Services Committee a report on Thursday saying all but about 35 pages of logs kept during the war on chemical weapon attack alarms and whether gas was found have been lost.

It estimated that the logs filled about 200 pages and said its investigation found that a computer virus destroyed some and that other pages and backup computer disks were lost when Gulf War records were shipped home after the war to the U.S. Central Command's headquarters in Tampa, Florida.
It said other military unit reports show no evidence that any U.S. soldier suffered nerve gas effects throughout the war, although it said many of those reports also were lost.

Gulf War Commander Gen. Norman Schwarzkopf told the panel he doubted U.S. troops were exposed to war gas because he never received any report either that war gas had been detected or that any U.S. soldier had been injured by it.

But the Defense Department announced last year that up to 20,000 U.S. troops may have been exposed to low levels of gas just after the war, when U.S. army engineers blew up an Iraqi weapons dump that contained chemical weapons.

The new Defense Department report on logs supports its argument last year against an allegation that logs on the eight critical days of the March 1991 Iraqi weapons dump demolition had disappeared. The new report disclosed that in fact most of the logs had been lost.

A separate study given to the Senate Armed Services Committee said investigation of other Gulf War unit reports found no evidence anyone was injured by war gas but many of those papers also have been lost.
"We have no evidence that any records were destroyed in any way to cover up or hide information bearing on Gulf War illnesses," the study said.
